segments.text: - Hello, everybody.
Welcome back to "Altium Academy."
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today we're gonna be
answering your questions

that came in on our recent
video about drill drawings.

Now, when we put out this
video on drill drawings,

we got some really good
questions about drill drawings
specifically as well as the role

of fabrication drawings more
broadly in PCV manufacturing.
So that's what we're gonna look at today,

and we'll even look at some
example fabrication drawings,

fabrication notes, and drill
drawings to really show
what these drawings are used for.
Let's go ahead and hop in and get started.
(upbeat music)
Now, as I mentioned in the introduction,

we put out a video about
creating drill tables recently,

and in that video we
got some great questions

from folks in the audience
asking about what is the role

of a drill drawing as well
as fabrication drawings,
more generally.
The fabrication drawing for your PCB

holds all of the requirements
needed to manufacture that PCB
with any fabrication house,
and that's really the whole point
of creating a fabrication drawing.
The other reason is that it functions
as a check against the data
that you export from your PCB layout,

and we'll see how that
arises here in just a moment.

But first, let's take a look
at those viewer questions.
Inductive Thinking writes,

"Do manufacturers even
look at drill drawings?

"I have the suspicion that
most PCB manufacturers

"just look at the
Gerbers, maybe some notes

"and completely ignore
all additional files.

"Some low cost Chinese
sites even explicitly state
"that they will only look at the Gerbers."

Well Inductive Thinking, I
can tell you certainly yes,

manufacturers do look
at a fabrication drawing
if you supply one.

Now, some PCB manufacturer
websites have a quote form
that you can fill out
and you can specify things like plating.

You can specify, for
example, minimum hole size,
your target line width and spacing,

those types of requirements
in the quote form.
And the primary purpose of that quote form

is to give you a price
estimate very quickly,
but at the end of the day,

they still have to look
at the files you give them

in order to give you a solid
quote for building that board.
Now, if you include a fabrication drawing
in your file package, they will look
at that fabrication drawing.

And one of the things
that they're looking for
is to see if any of the specifications
in your fabrication drawing differ
from what you put into their quote form
and to see if those specifications differ

from what they see in
the PCB file outputs.

T-Augie99 writes, "Why
would the fabricators
"want to see these drawings?

"I mean, for complex designs,
is it even understandable?

"And I'm sure nobody
would be drilling manually

"or even using semi-automatic
'cause it could cause errors.
"Or maybe I am wrong.

"I just don't know much
about the fabrication end
"of PCB manufacturing."

Now that question is
specifically referencing

a drill drawing, but of
course a drill drawing
is part of your fabrication drawing.
And I can tell you with certainty, no,

they are not using the drill
drawing for manual drilling
of all of the holes in your PCB.

One of the things they're
doing with that drill drawing
is again, they're using it as a check
against the NC drill data
that you export from your PCB layout file

and they can see graphically
where the drills should be

and they can use that as a
check against the numerical data
that comes in that NC drill file.

The other thing that you can
specify in a drill drawing
is of course tolerances.
And those tolerances are very important,

especially if you have
tight positional tolerances

and they need to know
if that's a requirement
that you have on that board
because if they deviate too much

from those positional tolerances,
then you might raise hell

with them and want to
have the boards rebuilt.
Now, as we'll see momentarily,

you want to also include
the dimensions of the PCB

as well as the dimensions of
any slots, any tooling sizes,

and then the dimensions
of any cutouts in the PCB
when you create your drill drawing.

So I can tell you with
confidence that yes,

if you supply a fabrication
drawing with your file package

to a PCB manufacturer,
they will look at it

and they will use it as
a master specification.

Now let's take a look at
an example drill drawing

for a project that I've
shown in some other videos

and we can really see why
this document is so important.
Now here I'm inside of Altium Designer

and you can see here I have
a fabrication drawing open
using the Draftsman tool.

When we just scroll
through the pages quickly,
we can see that we have all of the data
that a manufacturer would need

to understand what we want
to build in this project.

Now, some of the important
data that we have

that causes our fabrication
drawing to function

as a master specification
are really three things.

One of those is of course the
stackup drawing right here.
Now, if you're doing anything

where you're selecting a
specific material for your PCB,

then you need to provide
a stackup drawing.
Now it is standard practice to put

that stackup drawing into
the fabrication drawing
because it is of course something

that they will be fabricating
from base materials.

So you want to include that
in the fabrication drawing
as I've done here.

The other piece of information
that we have in here
that causes our fabrication drawing
to be the master specification for PCB
is of course the fabrication notes.
And inside the fabrication notes,
you can see all of the specifications
that we might put into a quote form
on the manufacturer's website.
Now, I've shown, just as an example,

the quote form from Sunstone
Circuits many times.
The quote form from Sunstone Circuits

asks you about a lot of these
aspects that you see here
in the fabrication notes.
So for example, the solder mask color.
What is the plating finish
that you want on exposed conductors?

What's the copper weight?
What is the overall thickness?
Now the fabrication notes allow you
to go a little bit deeper

because you can see here
in the fabrication drawing,

I am specifying tolerances
in my fabrication notes.

That's very important because
a lot of professional projects
are going to have mechanical tolerances

that need to be enforced in
different areas of the board.

And the fabrication drawing
is the place you specify

that, you don't really
specify that in a quote form.
Some other information that we see here

in the fabrication notes
that cause this document

to be the master
specification for our design

are, for example, found
right here in Note 11.

Here this gives some more detail
on the specific dielectric
that we're looking for.
This is a Rogers 4835,
but we're specifically asking
for an Unreinforced Rogers 4835

with a specific copper
applied to the base material.

Now, this is really
important in some designs
because that Unreinforced Rogers 4835

with that specific low-pro
copper is gonna be required
in this type of project

because this is a millimeter
wave sensor board.

And then for example here,
cap and filling on vias.

This isn't always
specified on quote forms.

This is something that you
would have to put into a note
and send over to the manufacturer.
And so of course you would want
to include it in the fabrication notes
and leverage your fabrication drawing

as the master specification
for your project.
The third major piece of information
that causes our fabrication drawing
to be like a master specification

is of course this drill
table and this drill drawing
and taken together,

this tells the manufacturer
where all of these via spans

that you see in the stackup
drawing are located in the PCB.

Now, one of the things
that the fabrication house

is going to do when
they look at your design

is they're going to open up
all of your fabrication data
and they're going to compare that

to your master specification
just to make sure
that there's no disagreements.

Whenever any of those files
don't match each other,

they're then gonna send you an
email asking you to clarify,
and you are gonna have to make a decision
which way you want to go with the design.

So for example, if I were
to send them a design
that specified 409

of these blind vias in
this fabrication drawing,
but my drill drawing contained 500 vias,
then they're gonna ask me, "Hey,
"why does your NC drill data mismatch
"from your fabrication drawing?"
Because again, the fabrication drawing

is the master specification
that's being used
to build the board.

Now, just as an example, when
we look at the drill table
and the drill drawing,

we can actually pull
open the NC drill data

and they can very quickly
compare the number of drill hits
of each size to the number

of drill hits specified
in the NC drill file.

So for example, you can
see here that we have all

of the drill sizes listed
here in this first part
of the NC drill file.
You can see here that the 0.0374 drill,

that is this entry right
here in the drill table,
that's the 37.402 mil plated holes.

And if we go back here,
we see that this is T13,
so we can find T13 using the search bar.

And then you can see
here, if we scroll down
to this lower part of the drill file,
we just count up the number of holes here.
You can see that there are nine holes

specified in the NC drill
file, and there are nine holes
specified in our drill table.
So great, that part of the data aligns.
So this is some of the review
that the CAM department is going to do
when they receive your file package

just to make sure that
your master specification

and your manufacturing
files are all in alignment.

So we've covered the information
in a fabrication drawing

that causes your drawing to be
like the master specification
for your design.

But it was mentioned
in one of the questions

that some low-cost Chinese
manufacturers will only review

the Gerbers, they won't
review a fabrication drawing.

So how do you get this
fabrication information

in front of them if they're
only going to be looking
at Gerber files?
Well, there is a way to do that.

What you can do is you can
put the fabrication data

into the PCB layout file as
I'm showing here on screen.
So if I just change the view color here,
it's gonna be a little bit easier to see.
We'll go ahead and make it white.

Now, what you can see here
in this fabrication drawing
is we've put a title block.
We've put all of the fabrication data

directly into the PCB layout
file in a mechanical layer.
And you can see right here it's been put
into the drill drawing layer.
So the drill drawing layer
is not just all your drill symbols.
You can actually put

all of this additional
fabrication information
into that drill drawing layer.
How do you get this into a Gerber file?
Well, that's very simple.

If we just go up here to
File, Fabrication Outputs
and then we select Gerber Files,
we can then export a Gerber file

that just contains this
drill drawing information.

Now of course, when I bring
up the Gerber setup dialogue,
you can see here all of the copper layers,
silk screen, solder mask

and paste mask are all
brought up by default.
But if we just scroll down here,

we can select Drill Drawing
right here on the right hand
side with this checkbox.

If we include that drill
drawing in the export,
it is gonna put all of the data
that you see here in this drill drawing
as well as all of the drill symbols,

and take that and put
it into a Gerber file,

and you can include that Gerber
file with your file package
that you provide to that manufacturer.
Now, I am personally a fan of PDF files

because oftentimes you have to
send that fabrication drawing

to someone who doesn't
have a Gerber viewer
just so that they can look at it.

So you shouldn't really expect
that everyone's gonna be able
to look at your Gerber files.

But what you can do if you are
gonna send this file package

to a manufacturer is you
can really just export both.

You can export your
fabrication drawing as a PDF,

and then you can create
an exact copy of that
as a Gerber file using the method here
that I've shown on screen.
That way you can make sure
that the manufacturer has both files
and they can use whatever file they want.
Thanks for watching this video, everybody.

I'm gonna try and do more
videos on data management,
including manufacturing data management,

because it is very important
if you're transitioning

from hobby project to
professional projects.
Make sure to hit that like button,

hit that subscribe button,
leave your comments
and questions in the comments section,

and don't forget to call
your fabricator folks.
We'll see you next time.
(upbeat music)

title: Do PCB Manufacturers Actually Look at Fabrication Drawings?
